Seven cases of hantavirus have been identified after a suspected outbreak on a luxury cruise ship off West Africa that has killed three people. The World Health Organization says there are two confirmed cases and five suspected cases on the ship, carrying mostly British, American and Spanish passengers. “As of May 4, 2026, seven cases (two laboratory confirmed cases of hantavirus and five suspected cases) have been identified, including three deaths, one critically ill patient and three individuals reporting mild symptoms,” the WHO said. About 150 people are still stuck on the vessel after a Dutch couple and a German national died, and others fell ill, including a Briton who left the vessel and was being treated in South Africa, authorities said. Medics were working on Monday to evacuate two people with symptoms of the virus. The Netherlands’ National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM), which is assisting with the outbreak, said hantavirus had been confirmed in one of the patients showing symptoms. But authorities in the island nation of Cape Verde said they had not allowed Dutch-flagged MV Hondius to dock as a precaution. Seven cases of hantavirus have been confirmed about the MV Hondius off the coast of Cape Verde. “We’re not just headlines: we’re people with families, with lives, with people waiting for us at home,” Jake Rosmarin, a US travel blogger, said in a tearful Instagram video post from the ship on Monday. Oceanwide Expeditions was trying to arrange the repatriation of two crew members with symptoms of the disease — one British and one Dutch — along with the body of the German national and a “guest closely associated with the deceased” who does not have symptoms. Spanish authorities said they had not yet received a request for the ship to dock and disembark passengers there. South Africa’s Health Department confirmed two of the dead were Dutch nationals: a 70-year-old man, who died on St Helena on April 11, and his wife, 69, who died in South Africa after collapsing at OR Tambo International Airport.

# 7 Suspected Hantavirus Cases Aboard Cruise Ship MV Hondius. A serious public health incident is unfolding aboard the cruise vessel MV Hondius in the Atlantic Ocean, where seven suspected cases of hantavirus have been reported—including three deaths and one British passenger currently in intensive care, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Of these cases, two have been confirmed through laboratory testing; the remaining five are under investigation to determine whether they are linked. ## Ship Held Off Cape Verde Amid Quarantine. The MV Hondius remains anchored off the coast of Cape Verde, under quarantine. Local authorities have prohibited passenger disembarkation to protect public health. Oceanwide Expeditions, the operator of the vessel, described the situation as controlled and noted that the atmosphere onboard remains calm, with most passengers staying composed. ## ‘We Just Want to Go Home’. American passenger Jake Rosmarin shared a powerful video on social media, appealing for empathy and support. Speaking to his roughly 44,000 followers, he emphasized the human reality behind the headlines: “We’re not just a news story or a headline. We’re people—with families and lives waiting for us back home.” He described mounting psychological strain, citing uncertainty as the hardest part. “All we want is to feel safe, to get clear answers—and to go home.” He closed his message by asking for “kindness and understanding” from those following the situation. ## About Hantavirus. Hantavirus is typically transmitted to humans through contact with rodent droppings, saliva, or urine. Among the three fatalities reported so far are a Dutch couple and a German passenger; it has not yet been confirmed whether all deaths were caused by hantavirus. A 69-year-old British man is hospitalized in critical but stable condition at a hospital in South Africa, where infection with a hantavirus variant has been confirmed. Additionally, two crew members are exhibiting acute respiratory symptoms and require urgent medical attention—though the cause remains unconfirmed. Authorities are also considering relocating the ship to the Canary Islands to facilitate safe disembarkation and comprehensive medical evaluations. # Hantavirus-hit MV Hondius cruise ship to sail to Spain; rare Andes strain confirmed. JOHANNESBURG — A luxury cruise ship hit by a deadly hantavirus outbreak and marooned for days off the coast of Cape Verde with close to 150 people on board was due to head to Spain, while South Africa confirmed it identified among the victims a strain of the virus that can—in rare cases—spread among humans. And the Swiss government said a man who returned to Switzerland after being a passenger on the MV Hondius was infected with the hantavirus and was being treated in Zurich. A Dutch couple and a German national who had been on the ship have died, while a British national is in intensive care in South Africa. The Netherlands is preparing to evacuate three patients who are on board. Since the start of the outbreak, the World Health Organization has stressed that the risk to the broader public is low. But a limited spread among close contacts has been observed in some previous outbreaks with the Andes strain, which has spread in South America, including Argentina, where the cruise trip started in March. A presentation seen by Reuters said tests done by South Africa's National Institute for Communicable Diseases revealed that the Andes strain was the cause of infection in the Dutch woman who died in Johannesburg as well as in the British man who is still in hospital there. "This is the only strain that is known to cause human-to-human transmission, but such transmission is very rare and as said earlier, it only happens due to very close contact," the presentation said. The Philippines is ready to test for the hantavirus if the 38 Filipino crew members on board the ship are repatriated, the Department of Health said. Late on Tuesday, the Spanish Health Ministry said it had been asked by the World Health Organization and the European Union to take the MV Hondius and had given its agreement "in accordance with international law and humanitarian principles.". Meanwhile, the Dutch foreign ministry said it was coordinating the evacuation of three patients, one of them with Dutch nationality, to the Netherlands, where they will be provided with care.

results.title: Hantavirus outbreak sparks misinformation on ship passenger nationalities | Fact Check
results.content:
"Shocking! Hantavirus outbreak on MV Hondius spreading rapidly: 23 passengers have already disembarked early and returned to locations all around the world," reads a simplified Chinese X post published May 7, 2026.

"They are from: Australia, Taiwan, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands."

The post, which has been viewed over 73,000 times, includes a screenshot from a New York Post article that was translated into Chinese.

It cites a report from Spanish newspaper El Pais, quoting an anonymous passenger, that nearly two dozen people got off at the remote British island of Saint Helena before the WHO confirmed the outbreak.

They were supposedly able to return to their countries without undergoing strict isolation measures. [...] Similar claims spread on Threads, Instagram and Weibo as reports emerged that a rare outbreak of hantavirus had hit the MV Hondius cruise ship travelling from Argentina to Cape Verde (archived link).

A total of 11 cases have been reported, including three deaths aboard the Dutch-flagged vessel. Eight patients have tested positive for the Andes virus, the only strain transmitted between humans, the WHO said (archived link).

Hantavirus typically spreads from the urine, faeces and saliva of infected rodents.

There are currently no vaccines or specific treatments for the disease.

All known cases in the current outbreak were people aboard the cruise ship, and the WHO has said the risk to the general population is "absolutely low" (archived link).

## 'Inaccurate' report [...] ## 'Inaccurate' report

Taiwan's Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said on May 8 it checked with Dutch and Argentinian authorities, as well as the WHO, and found there were "no Taiwanese citizens" onboard MV Hondius (archived link).

The health agency called the anonymous passenger's report to El Pais "inaccurate".

AFP reached out to El Pais, as well as the New York Post, but responses were not forthcoming.

The ship's operator Oceanwide Expeditions said 32 passengers disembarked at Saint Helena a week before the outbreak was reported -- not 23 as the online posts claimed (archived link).

They include a passenger from New Zealand currently undergoing quarantine in Taiwan, the island's CDC said on May 15, adding the person tested negative for Andes hantavirus (archived link).
